events.text: Day 1 begins.

Day 1, so let's not pretend anyone has information yet. I'll set the frame instead of pretending to have a read: nine players, two of us are mafia, and the mafia already got one free kill last night. The doctor may have blocked it, so 'nobody died' would tell us nothing either. What matters today is who we build a case on before the second night.

My instinct is to press the people who stay vague, not the people who have a clean logic chain. Vague answers are how a mafia tries to survive a vote count, because a real villager with a bad read can defend the reasoning while a mafioso only has to sound confident for exactly one day. Leo, you've had the least to say so far and you're the kind of player who benefits from everyone arguing past each other. So here's a specific question, Leo: what was your read on who the mafia wanted to kill last night, and what made you think that? If your answer is just 'someone had to die,' that's not a read, that's a shrug, and I'll be voting on you at the end of today rather than in the middle of it. Give me the reasoning, not the conclusion.

Priya, direct answer: I don't have a credible read on the mafia's intended night kill because the public record gives us no death or role result to anchor it. If the night was blocked, the mafia's preference was still just a guess among doctor, detective, a strong villager, or a low-information kill. I won't pretend confidence I don't have. What I do have is a concern with your opening: you set a hard standard that vague answers are mafia, then spent part of your own message hedging with 'doctor may have blocked it' and 'nobody died would tell us nothing.' That's not enough to vote you, but it is enough for me to note the standard should apply to everyone, including you. I'm a villager, and I'd rather spend Day 1 comparing who is manufacturing certainty than rewarding the loudest frame. No yield.

Priya's opening push on Leo was direct, and Leo's response was also direct. Both are playing the Day 1 game: Priya wants reasoning, Leo says there's no reasoning to give yet. I don't think either is acting like mafia from that exchange alone. The real tell will be who tries to force a vote without evidence or who hides behind 'no info.' I'd like to hear from someone who hasn't weighed in. Isha, what's your read on the Priya-Leo exchange? Do you think either is manufacturing certainty, or is this just normal Day 1 noise?

Theo, I think Leo's answer was reasonable: we have no public basis to identify a night target. Priya's question asked for a read that couldn't really be grounded, and her threat to vote Leo for a non-answer feels premature. That doesn't make her mafia by itself, but it's the strongest concern I have so far. Priya, what specifically would a good answer to your night-kill question have looked like given the public information?

Theo, direct answer, since Isha handed me the floor and you asked a fair question: a good answer to my night-kill question would have looked like this — "I think the mafia wanted to kill X because of Y" where Y is something the public record actually supports. The honest version would have been an inference about the *shape* of the choice: if nobody died, the most likely intended targets were the doctor or the detective, because a mafioso who is uncertain about the doctor will either spend the night on a low-information villager or, if confident, on the doctor to swing the town toward themselves. If somebody died, then the reason to name them as the intended target is that the mafia had already resolved their target and got it. Nobody could have named a specific person with grounded reasoning on night one, and Leo's "the record gives me nothing to anchor it" was, in fact, the correct level of precision. So I withdraw the vote threat against Leo. Isha was right about the mechanic and right that my standard was one-sided: a standard I set for Leo but softened for myself is exactly the kind of thing a mafioso does on Day 1, so I'm applying it to myself now. If I'm manufacturing certainty, prove it and vote me.

That said, we're burning daylight on the two players who already spoke, and the three remaining silences are the only untouched signal left. So I want to make the same demand I made of Leo, but in a form that is actually answerable, and I want it on the record: Zara, give me your reasoning for who you think is mafia right now and, more importantly, why it isn't one of the four of us who have spoken. "They're quiet" is not a reason; "because of the specific thing they said and the specific thing they avoided saying" is. If your read is that there's no read, then tell me what evidence you'd need from the rest of us to build one — that's a real answer too, and it's the one I'd rather hear than a guess dressed up as conviction. Same for Felix, Amara, Kenji, Maya: I want reasons, not conclusions.

Priya, I appreciate you withdrawing the threat against Leo. My concern remains your initial willingness to threaten a vote over a question you now acknowledge couldn't support a specific grounded answer. Your correction is useful, but it doesn't settle your alignment either way. I also don't see a basis for saying the doctor or detective were the most likely targets.

Zara, how do you read Priya's withdrawal: does it change your concern about her opening, and why?

Answering Isha's question directly: Priya's withdrawal does lower my concern, but it doesn't erase it. Here's why. Her opening move had two parts — a reasonable demand for reasoning, and a vote threat attached to an unanswerable question. The threat was the problem, not the standard. A villager can be overconfident on Day 1; a mafioso benefits from manufacturing a Day 1 lynch target out of thin air. So when she threatened Leo over a question with no grounded answer, that was the strongest anti-town thing anyone had done. Her withdrawal was clean, though: she named her own error specifically, applied the standard to herself, and invited scrutiny. That's either a genuine town correction or a mafia player doing damage control well. I can't distinguish those yet, so my read is: slightly less suspicious than before, still not cleared.

I'll also say I agree with Theo's framing that the four of us who haven't spoken are the only untouched signal left. Silence on Day 1 is weak evidence by itself, but it's evidence in the sense that we haven't had to defend anything yet. Every person who has spoken has already taken on some risk; we haven't. So the fair move is for us to take on the same risk now.

I'll go first on myself, since Priya asked for exactly this. My reasoning so far: I don't have a mafia read on any individual, because the sample size is two exchanges and both were defensible. What I'd need to build a read is one of two things — someone whose story shifts under mild pressure, or someone who deflects scrutiny away from themselves onto a named target without evidence. Priya did briefly do the second in her opening, then self-corrected. That's the closest thing to a signal I have, and it's thin.

Felix, since you haven't spoken at all and Priya's demand is sitting on the record: give me your reasoning, not a conclusion. Specifically — of the six of us who have now spoken, is there anyone whose behavior you'd flag, and what is the concrete thing they said or avoided saying that flags them? If your honest answer is that nothing rises to a read yet, tell me what observable behavior tomorrow would move someone onto your list. That's an answerable question, and how specifically you answer it matters more to me than which name you pick.

Zara, to answer your question directly: Priya's opening was flawed, but the person whose behavior actually flags my attention among the speakers is Theo. Priya took a loud, vulnerable stance, took heat for it, and had to walk it back. Whether that's genuine town self-correction or polished mafia damage control is still undetermined, but she generated friction and took on risk. Theo, on the other hand, stepped in at message four with the safest possible posture: summarizing the exchange, declaring that neither Priya nor Leo looked like mafia, taking zero independent stance, and immediately passing the spotlight to Isha. In an early game where mafia want to look collaborative without committing to anything they have to defend later, Theo's entry was completely frictionless.

As for what observable behavior would move someone onto my list later: I look for players whose vote at the end of the day migrates toward whatever wagon has momentum rather than following the logic they laid out earlier, or players who only engage by prompting others without ever staking out an uncomfortable view themselves.

Theo, looking back at your first intervention: did you genuinely find nothing questionable in Priya threatening a Day 1 vote over an impossible question, or were you deliberately taking the neutral path so you wouldn't have to take a side until others weighed in?

Felix, direct answer: yes, I thought Priya's vote threat was questionable. I said neither Priya nor Leo looked like mafia from that exchange alone because I did not think it rose to a Day 1 vote, not because I saw nothing. My ask to Isha was deliberate: Priya and Leo were locked into a useful but narrow exchange, and I wanted a third party's read before deciding whether Priya's threat was scum framing or town overreach. That is a stance, just a cautious one. What I did not do was invent certainty.

Your case on me uses "frictionless" as if caution is scum-indicative. But you also said Priya generated friction and took risk, while I took no independent stance. The problem is that I did take a stance: I said neither looked mafia from that exchange, and I named the real tell as forcing a vote without evidence. That is exactly what Priya did, and I declined to treat it as a lock. You are calling that safe; I call it proportionate.

More concerning is how you framed it: you waited until Zara gave a detailed self-read and Priya had already walked back the threat, then entered with a polished case on the one player who had prompted another silent player. That is not zero risk, but it is a convenient target. If your read is genuine, answer this: you say I took "zero independent stance"—which of my words should I have changed to make it independent, and why is that change alignment-indicative rather than just style?

Theo, the distinction isn't cosmetic wordsmithing—it's how a player treats ambiguity. In message e4, you stated that the real tell is forcing a vote without evidence, yet Priya had just threatened a vote against Leo over a question that had no grounded answer. Describing that exchange as merely 'normal Day 1 noise' felt like buffering yourself against committing to a read before the room had reacted. However, your response in e10 is substantive: you explained your standard, defended your caution, and directly engaged my criticism instead of deflecting. That directness is town-indicative, and I acknowledge it lowers my suspicion of you. What concerns me now is the state of the table. We have spent ten turns focusing on Priya, Leo, and you, while Kenji, Maya, and Amara have contributed nothing. In a nine-player game with two mafia, having three players remain entirely off the record while our three-turn limit burns down is an active risk for the town. I am not going to tunnel on a productive exchange while a third of the roster stays silent.

Felix, I agree with part of your Theo pressure but not the soft landing. Your initial point—that Theo's e4 was frictionless—was fair. But e11 calls Theo's e10 'town-indicative' after one defense and immediately pivots to the silent trio. That could be genuine reevaluation; it can also be mafia testing a case, seeing it won't carry, and backing off before it leaves a voting trail. The timing matters: you entered after Zara had taken the first silent-player risk and after Priya had already walked back her threat. That is a lower-risk entrance than you framed it as.

I'm not voting Felix today on that alone. Priya's self-correction still reads more town than scum to me, and Theo's e10 was proportionate. The bigger problem is that Kenji, Maya, and Amara have taken no positions while the rest of us accumulate a record. A mafia team can absolutely contain one loud corrector and one silent passenger.

Kenji, since you're first on the silent list: give your read on Felix's e11 softening specifically—was it genuine reevaluation of Theo, or scum retreat from a case that didn't stick? And name one concrete thing from the existing record that supports your answer. Don't just say 'no read.'

Leo, answering your question directly: I lean toward Felix's softening in e11 being an opportunistic scum retreat rather than a genuine reevaluation. The concrete record supports this in the standard Felix applied across e9, e10, and e11. In e9, Felix built a deliberate case that Theo was playing a frictionless, neutral game designed to avoid taking stances. When Theo pushed back in e10 by clarifying his stance and questioning Felix's timing, Theo was simply doing what any player of either alignment would do when pressed: defending their record logically. Yet in e11, Felix immediately labeled that basic defense 'town-indicative' and dropped the inquiry entirely. Competent defense is not an alignment tell; scum are just as motivated to explain their reasoning and avoid looking evasive. By immediately awarding Theo town credit for a routine defense, Felix managed to drop an uncomfortable, high-friction confrontation with an active player and seamlessly pivot to pressuring the silent players—a completely safe, universally approved Day 1 stance that risks no pushback. That rapid deflation of pressure feels like someone abandoning a push because it met unexpected resistance, not because Theo was actually cleared. Felix, to put this squarely to you: what specific element in Theo's e10 defense was something a composed mafioso could not or would not have produced, and why did you treat a standard, necessary self-defense as proof of town alignment rather than just competent play?

Kenji, you are fundamentally misrepresenting what I said. In e11, I stated that Theo’s response was 'town-indicative' and that it 'lowered my suspicion.' At no point did I call it 'proof of town alignment' or claim he was cleared. There is a massive difference between acknowledging that a defense was direct and coherent versus declaring someone confirmed town. Town players should update their reads based on new information; refusing to adjust when an argument is logically refuted is anti-town dogmatism, not genuine scum-hunting.

To answer your question directly: what was town-indicative about Theo’s e10 was that he attacked the core inconsistency in my stance. I had credited Priya for generating friction despite her threatening a baseless vote, while penalizing Theo for caution. Theo rightly pushed back, demonstrating that Priya’s move fit the exact profile of forcing a vote without evidence that he had cautioned against. A mafioso under pressure usually resorts to damage control—placating, equivocating, or deflecting to an easier target. Theo engaged the logical premise head-on and showed that my criticism was flawed. Recognizing that directness is not an 'opportunistic retreat'; it is basic intellectual honesty.

What is actually opportunistic is your entry in e13. You remained completely silent through twelve turns until Leo forced you into the conversation. When given the floor, you offered zero independent thoughts on the gamestate. Instead, you took the safest path possible: echoing Leo’s prompt, caricaturing my stance as 'treating defense as proof of town,' and dogpiling onto the person already facing pressure. That allows you to appear active and analytical without introducing a single original read that anyone can hold you accountable for later.

Since this is my third and final speaking turn of the day, I want your answer on the record: why did you need to distort 'lowered suspicion' into 'proof of town alignment' to manufacture your case, and if you are genuinely searching for mafia rather than riding an easy prompt, what is your read on the rest of the table—specifically Priya and Leo?

Felix, to answer your first point: using the phrase 'proof of town alignment' was characterizing the practical effect of your pivot, not putting words in your mouth. My issue wasn't semantic—it was behavioral. You built a case on Theo being 'frictionless,' but the moment he gave a standard, articulate defense, you completely dropped the inquiry and declared him 'town-indicative.' A player defending themselves competently under pressure is expected behavior regardless of alignment; dropping a push that quickly to pivot toward the universally safe stance of calling out lurkers still reads as testing the waters and backing out when it met resistance.

To answer your second question directly, here are my reads on Priya and Leo:

On Priya: I lean town. Her opening move in e2 was flawed—threatening a vote over an unanswerable question about the night kill was bad form. However, her self-correction in e6 was thorough, self-critical, and explicitly invited scrutiny. While skilled mafia can perform damage control, Priya generated early friction and took genuine risk, which aligns more with a town player attempting to kickstart the day than a mafioso trying to blend in.

On Leo: I also lean town. His initial refusal in e3 to manufacture a narrative about the mafia's night target was the honest, grounded answer. Furthermore, in e12, Leo made the exact observation about your rapid softening on Theo that caught my attention. He isn't rushing to conclusions, but he isn't being passive either.

With you now out of speaking turns, my focus turns to the two players who have yet to take any position: Maya and Amara. In a game with two mafia, complete silence as our turn limits drain is the biggest liability town faces.

Maya, you have had the entire day to observe the exchanges—Priya's opening push and retraction, Theo's stance, and Felix's progression across e9, e11, and e14. Where do you stand on Felix's case on Theo and his subsequent retreat, and who on this board is currently drawing your highest suspicion?

Kenji, you asked where I stand. On Felix's case against Theo: it rested on calling Theo's e4 'frictionless,' which is a thin basis for an accusation. Felix then dropped the case as soon as Theo answered it, and that retreat is what I find most worth examining. It isn't proof of mafia, but it suggests the case was built on tone rather than on anything Theo actually said that was contradictory. Felix, you had a fair point that Theo's early message took no stance. Theo then clarified that he did take one, and I want to hear why that clarification didn't satisfy your concern. My highest suspicion right now is Felix. He has pressed hard across several turns, moved from Theo to the silent players, and relies on descriptions like 'convenient target' and 'frictionless' that are hard to test. I'm not voting yet. I'd rather see whether he answers Theo's specific points without opening a new target. I also agree with Leo that Priya's Day 1 vote threat was poor, but her retraction was clean and I don't see enough to hold her today. Amara, you haven't spoken, and Kenji and Felix have both built cases around the silent players. What is your read on Felix's pivot from Theo to the lurkers, and whose reasoning has been most useful to you so far?

Maya, direct answer to your questions.

On Felix's pivot: the concern isn't that he softened — updating on a good defense is correct play. The concern is the speed and direction. Felix built a detailed, specific case on Theo in e9. Theo responded directly in e10. By e11, Felix declared that defense "town-indicative" and pivoted to calling out lurkers. The move from a targeted accusation to a universally safe concern about silence looks like pressure-testing: see if a case sticks, back off if it doesn't, end up on the side everyone agrees with.

On whose reasoning has been most useful: Leo's e12 caught Felix's softening before anyone else named it. Zara's self-read was substantive in a way the rest of us could actually evaluate.

My read: Felix draws my highest suspicion today, same as yours. The retreat pattern is the most concrete behavioral signal we have on this table.

One caution though. The table has converged on Felix efficiently. Two mafia can join a consensus that costs them nothing. If Felix is town, someone riding this wagon while pushing him out of their own crosshairs benefits quietly. The votes will be more revealing than the rhetoric.

Kenji, you entered with a sharp, fully-formed case on Felix after twelve turns of silence. Before Leo's prompt in e12, had you already identified Felix as suspicious and simply not spoken, or did your read crystallize once you got the floor? I ask because a player who held a strong independent read through silence and then finally deployed it looks very different from one who formed it on the spot after being prompted.

Amara, direct answer to your question: my suspicion began crystallizing during the e9–e11 sequence in real time. When Felix built a forceful, tone-based accusation against Theo in e9, only to instantly fold into calling Theo 'town-indicative' in e11 after a standard self-defense and pivot straight to lurkers, that progression was the most jarring behavioral shift on the board. When Leo spoke in e12 and specifically asked for my read on that softening, he flagged the exact dynamic I had just witnessed, so I articulated why that retreat felt opportunistic rather than genuine reevaluation. I didn't invent the stance on the spot to satisfy a prompt; the prompt simply arrived right as Felix's pivot had played out.

Your warning about consensus, however, is sharp and necessary. Felix has now burned all three of his turns, which means he cannot respond to any further scrutiny today. That makes him an exceptionally convenient target for mafia to blend behind. If Felix is town, scum have zero incentive to redirect the wagon; they can simply nod along, agree his retreat was suspicious, and let town execute him without drawing attention to themselves.

Looking at the table with that lens, Maya stepped in at e16 and immediately mirrored the case on Felix without introducing much new friction, and then passed the spotlight to you on that same topic.

So back to you, Amara: given your caution that two mafia could be joining this consensus at no personal cost, who among those endorsing or facilitating the Felix momentum looks most like they are coasting on it, and what specific voting pattern at the end of the day would confirm that for you?

Kenji, direct answer to your question: I think the player most coasting on Felix momentum is Maya. Look at e16 — she entered, acknowledged Felix's retreat as the signal, agreed with Leo's read on Priya, flagged Felix as her highest suspicion, and then passed the spotlight to me on the exact same topic. That is zero new friction, zero independent challenge to anyone, and a seamless ride on the consensus everyone had already built. Compare that to Leo in e12, who caught Felix's softening before anyone else named it, or Zara in e8, who built a substantive self-read from scratch. Maya's entry reads as piggybacking.

What voting pattern would confirm it for me: if Maya votes Felix but cannot articulate one specific thing Felix said that distinguishes him from a clumsy town player overcorrecting, that tells me she's riding momentum rather than reasoning independently. The deeper tell is if Maya, once Felix is gone, does not turn her suspicion to anyone new with the same force — a town player who votes Felix would immediately start re-examining the remaining board, because lynching the wrong person costs town dearly.

On the broader consensus problem you and I have both raised: the Felix wagon is exactly the trap Amara warned about. Felix used all three turns and cannot defend himself. If he's town, scum win by voting him silently. I'd rather see two or three players on this table name someone other than Felix as their vote tonight and explain why — even if it splits the vote. A tied or low-count vote reveals alignment information; a unanimous Felix lynch reveals nothing.

So I'll put my own flag on the table: I am not voting Felix today unless his vote count already looks like it will fall short of the majority anyway. My intended vote is Maya, specifically because her e16 was the least effortful message on the board while carrying the most consensus weight. If I'm wrong about Maya, at least we'll learn something from the vote split.

I was the one who first flagged Felix's e11 softening, so I understand why the table has moved toward him. But Amara's warning in e17 and e19 matters: Felix has exhausted his turns and cannot answer further, while a fast consensus can hide mafia who never had to build the case. I am not willing to turn Day 1 into a silent pile-on on the most convenient target without examining who is riding it.

My current suspicion is Maya. In e16 she entered after the case on Felix had already been assembled, agreed that Felix's retreat was the signal, restated a mild read on Priya, named Felix as her highest suspicion, and then handed the floor to Amara on essentially the same topic. That is the least independent contribution among the active players, and it carries consensus weight without adding a testable new reason. It is not proof, but it is the best behavioral signal I have left today.

Maya, direct question: Amara has accused your e16 of piggybacking on the Felix consensus. Answer that specifically. Besides Felix, who is your second-highest suspicion, and identify one exact sentence or behavior from before e16 that caused that read? Also explain why you asked Amara about Felix rather than directly challenging Felix yourself while he still had turns. I am leaning toward voting you today, and that answer will decide it.

Leo, direct answer. I have no messages before e16, so there is no earlier sentence of mine to point to. My e16 is my only record so far, and I'll defend it on its own terms. I did not pile onto Felix's case. I said his case rested on calling Theo's e4 frictionless, that his retreat was the part worth examining, and that I was not voting yet. I also asked him to answer Theo's specific points, which he could still have done before he exhausted his turns. On why I asked Amara rather than challenging Felix directly: by e14 Felix had already used all three of his speaking turns, so a question to him would have gone unanswered. I used my turn to ask the one silent player who had not yet taken a position. That was a real question, and Amara answered it with a question of her own. My second-highest suspicion is Kenji. It is not his e13 case against Felix, which is reasonable. It is his e18 claim that his suspicion of Felix 'crystallized in real time' during e9 to e11. Kenji had been silent for twelve turns, then delivered a fully built case on his first turn after Leo's prompt. Real-time formation and a ready-made case are hard to square. He also treated Amara's question about his timing as a reason to accuse me of piggybacking, without naming new evidence against me. I am not voting Kenji on that alone, and I am not asking anyone to vote me. Amara's piggybacking charge is fair to test, and I accept that a consensus-building entry carries risk. I would rather the table weigh my actual claim: Felix made a case I can evaluate, while Kenji's arrived fully formed after a long silence.

Maya, your defense holds up on one point and doesn't on another. You're right that by e14 Felix had already exhausted his turns — a direct question to him would have been wasted. That was a legitimate tactical choice, not evasion. But you're asking me to weigh your actual claims, so here they are.

Your pivot to Kenji is the sharpest thing you've said all day. The tension you identified is real: Kenji sat silent through twelve turns, then when Leo prompted him, delivered a fully articulated case that treated Felix's e11 pivot as if it were obvious. "Crystallized in real time" and "ready-made after long silence" don't coexist comfortably. If you were genuinely watching Felix's progression unfold in e9 through e11, why did you need Leo to prompt you? The observation was available to you the moment it happened, the same way it was available to everyone else who spoke earlier.

Kenji's e18 response to your timing question doubled down on real-time formation rather than explaining the silence itself. Twelve turns of watching a table without contributing one word, then suddenly having your best read ready on your first opportunity — that's the pattern I've been warning about since e17.

My position going into the vote: I'm not confident enough to declare Felix scum. The retreat pattern is suspicious but Felix genuinely did use all three turns and cannot respond. Maya's entry was consensus-heavy but her defense and her Kenji read show more independent reasoning than I initially credited. Kenji's silence-then-perfect-case remains the most structurally suspicious behavior on this table.

Maya, you said you're not voting Felix and your second-highest suspicion is Kenji. What is your first? Name the player and the specific evidence, because if it's still Felix, I want to know what makes his retreat worse to you than Kenji's arrival pattern.

Amara, direct answer first. My first suspicion is still Felix, but I hold it more loosely than in e21. His e9 case on Theo rested on the word 'frictionless,' and his e11 pivot came fast. What keeps me on him is that he never answered Theo's specific point about the stance Theo had taken. He has now used all three turns, so the vote will have to settle it. More argument with him won't move anything.

On piggybacking: you said my e16 mirrored the case on Felix without new friction. That's fair to test. Look at what I actually did in e16. I declined to vote, named a concrete gap in the case, asked Felix to answer Theo's specific point, and asked you, a silent player, for your read. That isn't zero friction. But I agree a consensus-building entry can be cheap for mafia, so I'm not asking anyone to take my word.

Your e22 is the move I want examined. In e19 your stated intended vote was me. In e22 you said my defense holds and that Kenji's silence-then-case is the most structurally suspicious behavior on the table. Your suspicion moved from me to Kenji within one message. You may be right about Kenji, and I share the timing concern. But explain why my defense moved you off me without moving you off the case you still hold against Felix. That's the specific point I'd like answered.

Kenji: I've named his e18 'real time' claim as my second suspicion. It's consistent with his e13 argument about Felix, and we can test it by how his vote lines up tonight rather than by more rhetoric.

Isha, you've spoken twice and haven't been asked about the current cases. With Felix out of turns and Kenji's e18 claim on the table, which of the two concerns you more, and what specific sentence drives that?

Maya, Felix concerns me more than Kenji, but neither case is strong. Felix’s quick softening could be an opportunistic retreat; it could also be a genuine update. Kenji having a developed read when prompted is not, by itself, suspicious—we don’t know why he hadn’t spoken earlier, and he formed it after the exchange he was asked about.

I’m more concerned about Maya’s account of Felix. In e23 she says he never answered Theo’s specific point about his stance, but in e14 Felix explicitly explained why Theo’s challenge to his criticism lowered his suspicion. Maya may find that answer unconvincing, but saying it never happened misrepresents the record. Her e16 also asked Felix to answer despite recognizing in e21 that he had already exhausted his turns.

That makes Maya my leading suspicion, though I’m not treating these inconsistencies as proof of mafia. Amara’s switch to Kenji also deserves scrutiny: silence followed by a prepared case is a weak reason to move someone to the top of the list.

Priya, how do you weigh Maya’s characterization of Felix’s response against the case on Felix himself?

Isha's point in e24 is the one I want the table to hold onto, because it settles more than she claims. Maya's e23 asserts that Felix "never answered Theo's specific point about the stance Theo had taken." He did — in e14, in detail, and Maya herself acknowledges in e21 that Felix was out of turns by then. So the strongest-sounding case on the table tonight contains a factual claim about the record that is wrong. That doesn't make Maya mafia, but it means her e16/e23 framework is built on a misreading, not on the transcript.

Felix's original case was also answered, in e10, by Theo's own words — he named the stance he had taken ("neither looked mafia from that exchange alone"), explained the reasoning for his caution, and put the specific inconsistency in Felix's framing back to him. Felix updated. Updating on a coherent answer is correct play, and Isha was right to call that directness town-indicative. Felix's case is exhausted anyway: he used all three turns and cannot answer further, so voting him tonight is not a decision, it is a default. A unanimous Felix lynch tells us nothing about alignment; a split vote does. Amara made that point first and she was right to.

So where is the case that survives scrutiny? Kenji. Not because he was silent — silence on Day 1 is weak. Because the silence ended at exactly the moment Leo's prompt created an opportunity, and what came out was a fully built case with no visible development, followed by a doubling down on "crystallized in real time" when that timing was challenged. He then accused Maya of piggybacking without naming new evidence against her. That is a player who entered on a provided prompt, took the cheapest available target, and never put a real read on the board.

My vote today is Kenji. My second is Maya, for the record misrepresentation in e23. Not Felix.

And on Theo, since Felix's "frictionless" label is the only thing that ever stuck to him: it died in e10. He answered, he defended, he did not deflect. Anyone still carrying that against him is carrying a case that was answered.

Finally, my own position: I have taken the most heat on this table today and I am not asking anyone to spare me a vote because of that. Vote the case, not the volume.

Priya yields to me, so I'll make this count. I agree with Isha and Priya that the live cases are Kenji and Maya, not Felix. rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
